modules.title: Warm-up and queue refresher
goals: Add to the back of a queue and take from the front (first in, first out).
Read basic Python: a list by its index and a simple loop.

segments.title: Before we start
segments.body:
How does a social network find your friends of friends without checking every account it has? It starts from you and spreads out one ring of friends at a time. That search is **breadth-first search** (BFS), and by the end of this course you will have written it yourself.

BFS explores a graph **one ring at a time**, and to do that it keeps a **queue** of places still to visit. The code we will write and read uses Python **lists** and a **loop**.

This short warm-up checks what you already remember. Each question is followed by a short refresher on the same idea: if you got the question wrong or weren't sure, read it before you move on. Your answers here don't count towards any result or medal: they only show you what to read.

segments.title: Warm-up question: which item leaves the queue?
Refresher: how a queue works
segments.body:
A **queue** is **first in, first out** (FIFO): you add to the **back** and take from the **front**, like a line at a till. The person who joined first is served first.

Adding an item to the back is called **enqueueing** it (to **enqueue**), and taking the item at the front is **dequeueing** it (to **dequeue**). You will see both words in code and in books.

In Python a queue is a `collections.deque`:

```python
from collections import deque
q = deque()
q.append("A")     # add A to the back
q.append("B")     # add B to the back; queue is now A, B
first = q.popleft()  # take from the front -> "A"
```

`append` puts an item at the back, and `popleft` takes the item at the front. BFS uses exactly this: it adds the neighbours it finds to the back, and always visits the one at the front next.

segments.title: Refresher: lists and indexing
segments.body:
A **list** holds items in order, and you read one by its **index**, counting from 0:

```python
neighbours = ["B", "C", "D"]
neighbours[0]   # -> "B", the first item
neighbours[1]   # -> "C", the second item
```

The first item is at index `0`, not `1`. Later we store each vertex's neighbours as a list like this, so reading a list by its index is how we look at who a vertex connects to.

segments.title: Refresher: a for-loop over a list
segments.body:
A **for-loop** runs its body once for each item in a list, giving the item a name each time:

```python
for item in ["B", "C", "D"]:
    print(item)
```

This prints `B`, then `C`, then `D`: the loop variable `item` is `"B"` on the first pass, `"C"` on the second and `"D"` on the third. Later BFS loops over a vertex's neighbours this same way, taking one neighbour at a time.

segments.title: You're ready
segments.body: That's everything the warm-up checks: a **queue** (first in, first out), reading a **list** by its index, and a **loop** over a list. The next module shows what a graph actually is and builds on exactly these ideas.

activities.title: Which item leaves the queue first?

config.prompt: Three people join an empty queue: Ama joins, then Ben, then Cebo. Who is served first?

solution.explanation: A queue is first in, first out. Ama joined first, so she is at the front and is served first.

feedback.b: Not quite. Cebo joined last, so Cebo is served last. A queue is first in, first out. Ask: who joined first?
feedback.c: Not quite. Ben is in the middle. In a queue the person who joined first is at the front, and is served first. Ask: who has waited longest?

hints.body: A queue works like a real line of people. Who gets served first in a line?
A queue is first in, first out: the item that was added first comes out first.
Ama joined before Ben and Cebo.
Answer: Ama. She joined first, so she is at the front and is served first.

activities.title: Reading a list by its index

config.prompt: The list items is ["B", "C", "D"]. What is items[1]?

solution.explanation: Python counts list positions from 0. items[0] is "B", so items[1] is the second item, "C".

feedback.b: Not quite. "B" is items[0]: a list is indexed from 0, so index 1 is the second item. Count from 0 along the list.
feedback.c: Not quite. items[1] reads a single item at that index, not a slice of the list. Count from 0 to find the item at index 1.

hints.body: A list is indexed from 0, not 1.
items[0] is the first item, so items[1] is the second.
The list is ["B", "C", "D"]; count B as 0, C as 1.
Answer: "C". Index 1 is the second item in the list.

config.prompt: What does this loop print? It is written on one line: for x in ["B", "C", "D"]: print(x)

options.label: B then C then D, one per line
The letter x, printed three times

solution.explanation: The loop takes each item in turn and prints it, so you get B, then C, then D, one per line.

feedback.b: Not quite. x is the loop variable: each time round it holds the next item, so the loop prints the items, not the letter x. Ask: what does x hold the first time round?
feedback.c: Not quite. The loop runs its body once per item and prints each one on its own line, not the whole list at once. Ask: how many times does print(x) run?

hints.body: A for-loop runs its body once for each item in the list.
Each time round the loop, x is set to the next item in the list.
So the body print(x) runs three times, with x being "B", then "C", then "D".
Answer: it prints B, then C, then D, each on its own line.
